id_and_class.summary: Bhartṛhari, the 5th-century philosopher-grammarian, holds that ultimate reality is a single indivisible linguistic principle, Śabda-Brahman, and that the world is a real transformation of language. Consciousness is linguistic in nature, always self-aware, and no cognition occurs without the word.

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is language (śabda) in its deepest form. The Absolute is Śabda-Brahman, the Brahman whose essence is the Word, and the consciousness of all beings ‘is in the nature of the word’.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Objects and the physical world are a real transformation (pariṇāma) of the linguistic Absolute. Bhartṛhari draws no material distinction between intellect (buddhi) and pure consciousness (cit).
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not applicable (consciousness-as-language is the beginningless, endless ground from which the world proceeds)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Consciousness is never separate from the self-awareness ‘I am’, which is innate, linguistic and eternal. The very distinction between self and non-self is grammatical, marked by first-person and second-person verb forms.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Śabda-Brahman, the eternal linguistic Absolute; pure consciousness (cit); the intellect or cognizer (buddhi); acts of cognizing (jñāna); levels of speech from audible words to an undifferentiated inner unity.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: All knowledge is intertwined with words, so reality is always encountered as interpreted reality. Bhartṛhari also grounds the view in scripture and grammatical analysis.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Three forms of language that Bhartṛhari calls knots of consciousness: Vaikharī (audible, articulated speech), Madhyamā (inaudible inner speech) and Paśyantī (the unitary inner form in which all differentiation is lost). The Vedic tradition adds a fourth, Parā, which some scholars identify with pure consciousness and Śabda-Brahman.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Cognition, self-awareness, the structure of experience and the origin of the world.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Language is the substance of reality. The world arises as the Word unfolds from undifferentiated Paśyantī into differentiated, audible speech and its objects.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: The one linguistic Absolute manifests progressively as differentiated phonemes, words and objects. This transformation is real, unlike the illusion (vivarta or māyā) of Śaṅkara's later Advaita Vedanta.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Consciousness exists ‘within and without’ in all beings undergoing transmigration, as the connective tissue under every individual's cognitions.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: The linguistic Absolute is the cause of manifested phonemes and of the world's creation. In each mind, language makes cognition possible by articulating what is perceived.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: One indivisible linguistic principle underlies all cognitions, and at the level of Paśyantī every differentiation is lost.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Every cognition is shot through with words; perception is interpretation in terms of some language. Matilal glosses this as reality being ‘invariably’ interpreted linguistically.
core_claims_and_evidence: Bhartṛhari states that there is no cognition in the world in which the word does not figure.
The Absolute is qualified by language (Śabda-Brahman), unlike Śaṅkara's attributeless Brahman.
The world is a real transformation of language, not an illusion.
Self-awareness accompanies all consciousness, and the self/non-self distinction is grammatical.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical and scriptural: Sanskrit grammatical analysis, Vedic tradition and nondualist metaphysics.

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: The opening verse of the Vākyapadīya uses the verb vivartate for the Absolute's appearing as objects, which sits awkwardly with the reading that the world is a real transformation (pariṇāma) rather than an appearance (vivarta).
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Whether the fourth level, Parā, belongs to Bhartṛhari's own scheme or only to later tradition is disputed among scholars.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: A consistent nondualism in which reality, knowledge and self-awareness share one linguistic structure. It anticipates the Pratyabhijñā school of Kashmir Shaivism, which Kumar argues borrowed from Bhartṛhari without substantial change.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Bhartṛhari describes the consciousness of beings ‘going through transmigration’ as linguistic and eternal, which presupposes continuity beyond a single bodily life.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: Since the world proceeds from the eternal Word, each being's consciousness is a manifestation of the Absolute.
